pharm: Long-acting tetracycline that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 30S ribosomal subunit; highly lipophilic with good tissue penetration.
quick: 200 mg initially, then 100 mg every 12 h
May take with food; avoid dairy/antacids at the same time
Avoid - fetal tooth and bone effects
Avoid prolonged use; short courses limited data
Reduce total dose in significant impairment
Caution; risk of hepatotoxicity and DRESS
Vestibular symptoms, skin pigmentation, LFTs, autoimmune signs
summary: Minocycline is a long-acting, highly lipophilic tetracycline used for acne, respiratory and genitourinary infections, and various susceptible organisms including some atypicals and resistant staphylococci. It penetrates tissues well, including the CNS. It is more likely than other tetracyclines to cause vestibular side effects (dizziness, vertigo), skin/mucosal hyperpigmentation, and, with prolonged use, autoimmune reactions (drug-induced lupus, autoimmune hepatitis) and DRESS. Like all tetracyclines it is avoided in pregnancy and young children.
indications: Respiratory tract infections from susceptible organisms
Sexually transmitted infections including chlamydia, nongonococcal urethritis, and lymphogranuloma venereum
Rickettsial infections, brucellosis, and other susceptible infections
Meningococcal carrier state eradication and infections caused by susceptible Staphylococcus, including some MRSA (per labeling/guidelines)

dosage.d: 200 mg initially, then 100 mg every 12 h (or 50 mg every 6 h)
dosage.n: Max about 400 mg/day; not to exceed labeled limits

dosage.d: 4 mg/kg initially, then 2 mg/kg every 12 h
Weight-based about 1 mg/kg once daily (extended-release tablets)
dosage.n: Lower weight-based dose reduces vestibular side effects

dosage.d: 100 mg every 12 h for at least 5-7 days

admin: May be taken with food to reduce GI and oesophageal irritation
Take with a full glass of water and remain upright for at least 30 minutes
Separate from antacids, iron, calcium, magnesium, zinc, and dairy by 2-3 hours (chelation)
Swallow extended-release tablets whole; do not split, crush, or chew
Use sun protection because of photosensitivity
moa: Minocycline reversibly binds the 30S bacterial ribosomal subunit, preventing aminoacyl-tRNA from attaching to the mRNA-ribosome complex and thereby inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis (bacteriostatic). Its high lipophilicity gives excellent tissue and intracellular penetration. It also has non-antibacterial anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties, which contribute to its effect in acne and other inflammatory conditions.

absolute: Pregnancy (tooth/bone effects) and children under 8 years except specific serious infections

preg: Use during the second and third trimesters can cause permanent discoloration of the child's teeth and may impair fetal bone growth; minocycline is generally avoided in pregnancy unless no alternative exists for a serious infection.
lact: Passes into breast milk; absorption by the infant is limited by chelation with milk calcium. Avoid prolonged use; short courses have limited data, so weigh benefit against risk of tooth/bone effects.
renal: Reduce the total daily dose and/or extend intervals in significant renal impairment, since high tetracycline levels can cause azotaemia, hyperphosphataemia, and acidosis. Avoid excessive accumulation.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment and avoid concurrent hepatotoxins. Minocycline can cause hepatotoxicity, autoimmune hepatitis, and is implicated in DRESS; monitor liver function during prolonged therapy.

major: Penicillins (bacteriostatic agent may antagonise bactericidal action)
moderate: Antacids, iron, calcium, magnesium, zinc, bismuth (chelation reduces absorption)
Oral contraceptives (rare reports of reduced efficacy)
minor: Penicillin G (theoretical antagonism), antacids alter absorption timing
interactions.food: May be taken with food; avoid taking simultaneously with dairy or mineral supplements due to chelation.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol; avoid additional hepatotoxic exposures given the risk of liver injury.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false elevations of urinary catecholamines and can interfere with some laboratory tests.

emergency: Severe blistering skin reaction or DRESS
Severe vision changes from intracranial hypertension

monitoring: Vestibular symptoms and ability to drive
Liver function and autoimmune markers with prolonged therapy
counsel: Take with water and stay upright for 30 minutes to protect the food pipe
Dizziness and spinning sensations are common - avoid driving until you know how it affects you
Use sunscreen; long-term use can darken skin, gums, or teeth
Report rash with fever, swollen glands, severe headache, vision changes, or yellowing of skin
Do not take with milk, antacids, or iron/calcium tablets at the same time
pk: Well absorbed orally; effective levels within hours
Store at 20-25 C; protect from light and moisture
pearls: More vestibular side effects (dizziness/vertigo) than other tetracyclines - warn about driving
Long-term use causes blue-black pigmentation of skin, mucosa, teeth, and even bone/thyroid
Can trigger drug-induced lupus, autoimmune hepatitis, and DRESS - monitor on prolonged therapy
Avoid in pregnancy and in children under 8 years (tooth discoloration, bone effects)
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip it and continue your normal schedule - do not double up. Try to space doses evenly.
overdose: Overdose mainly causes nausea, vomiting, and dizziness and is rarely life-threatening. There is no specific antidote; treatment is supportive. Antacids or calcium/magnesium salts can reduce further absorption. Minocycline is not effectively removed by dialysis.
